# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

# Review of the 24-month follow-up of the Varden trial and Halden organisations

This is a good follow-up. It answers most of the open questions from the earlier documents:
- It adds a second, stricter measure of hours (system logs).
- It tests the meetings mechanism under a registered plan.
- It reports the counter-office waiting times against control offices rather than only before and after.
- It costs the coverage problem.
- It names the design of the four long-duration studies, which I had asked the meta-analysis to do.

Its two main corrections to earlier claims are well founded. The per-hour gain does not disappear, and the meta-analysis's "no decay" claim rested on weak studies.

The serious problems are these. Two control offices changed their practices partway through, which partly undermines the 24-month comparison. The mediation analysis is presented with more confidence than the design can support. And the Summary's headline mixes two different hours measures.

**Arithmetic.** The core figures check out:
- Timesheet hours: 0.966 / 0.88 gives +9.8%.
- Log hours: 0.966 / 0.89 gives +8.5%.
- Mediation shares: 47% + 18% + 35% = 100%.
- Halden subset: 96.8 / 86.6 gives +11.8%, matching 34.9 / 40.3 = −13.4%.

The per-hour confidence intervals are almost exactly the per-employee intervals divided by the hours ratio. That means uncertainty in the hours measure contributes nothing to them. This was the same minor issue in the 9-month report: the true intervals should be somewhat wider.

---

## Major issues

### 1. The control group changed partway through

At month 15, two of the seven control case-processing offices ran a "meeting audit" and saw output per hour rise by 4.1%. The report treats this as a curiosity, but it changes the comparison the trial depends on.

- **It biases the 24-month estimate toward zero.** Suppose offices are equally weighted and the 4.1% gain holds. Then the control average rises by about 1.2%, which lowers the treated-versus-control gain by about 1.1 points. The like-for-like decline from 12.5% to 9.8% is 2.7 points, so perhaps 40% of the apparent "fading" is the control group improving, not the treated offices declining.
- **It is probably spillover from the treated offices.** Control offices that independently arrived at the treated offices' main mechanism within the same county were most likely influenced by them.

**Fixes:**
- Report 24-month estimates with and without the two affected offices.
- Report results cut off at month 15.
- Report the treated offices' own trajectory over time, separately from the comparison with control.

The interpretation of decay in §3 and §5 should be qualified accordingly.

### 2. The Summary compares figures measured differently

The Summary says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months". Those figures come from two hours measures: 12.5% is from timesheets and 8.5% from system logs. The like-for-like comparison, which §3 reports correctly, is 12.5% to 9.8% on timesheets. That is a decline of about 22%, not 32%.

§5's "declined by about a quarter" is also slightly generous, and the decline is not statistically tested. The 9-month and 24-month confidence intervals overlap heavily (+6.9 to +18.4 versus +4.6 to +15.2). With the same offices measured twice, a test for change between the two time points is straightforward and should be reported.

"Consistent with some fading" is fair. "Declined" is stronger than the data show.

### 3. The mediation analysis is presented too confidently

- **"Confirms" overstates it.** Mediation with mediators that were measured, not assigned, cannot confirm a mechanism. The Limitations section says so, but the Summary does not. "Supports" would be accurate.
- **The intervals look too narrow for 14 offices.** The report mentions "a larger sample of office-months". Office-months are not independent, so the effective sample is still 14 offices. An interval of 28–66% for an indirect effect estimated from 14 offices suggests that office-level clustering may not have been fully accounted for. The report should state how the intervals were computed and whether they reflect clustering by office.
- **It does not settle the "post hoc" objection.** The hypothesis was generated from these same seven offices, and the test was registered at month 11, after the exploratory result was known. The 24-month data are new time periods but the same offices. A registered test is a real improvement, but this is confirmation within the same sample, not independent replication.
- **Where did the baseline meeting data come from?** The 9-month report said calendar data were collected only in month 6. This report gives baseline figures (7.4 and 7.2 hours). If these were recovered retrospectively from calendar history, say so, along with how complete that history was.

### 4. What do system logs measure?

The report describes log time as "time staff are working on cases". If it counts only work done in the case-management system, then:
- the log measure excludes meetings, and output per log-hour is roughly output per hour of casework;
- the most mechanical way that fewer meetings raise output, moving time from meetings to cases, does not register in output per log-hour. It is then unclear how meetings could explain 47% of the gain in that outcome;
- the figures do not fit together. Non-meeting time in treated offices fell only about 5% relative to control (see below), yet log hours fell 11%.

Here is the arithmetic, assuming timesheet hours include meetings and using a 37.9-hour baseline:

| | Timesheet hours | Meetings | Non-meeting hours |
|---|---|---|---|
| Treated | about 33.4 | 3.9 | about 29.5 |
| Control | about 37.9 | 7.0 | about 30.9 |

Non-meeting time is about 4.7% lower in treated offices, against output per employee 3.4% lower. That implies output per non-meeting hour roughly 1–2% higher. On timesheet hours, almost all of the gain is time moved out of meetings.

This supports the authors' central claim, arguably more strongly than their mediation estimate does. But it also means the report needs to say exactly what log time includes:
- meetings?
- idle time while logged in?
- work done outside the case system?

Without that, the log-based figures cannot be interpreted.

### 5. The backlog is still not reported

The 9-month report flagged backlogs and statutory deadlines as a risk. Two years of output per employee 3.4% below control would build a substantial queue if incoming cases were unchanged. Queue length, case age and on-time completion are available from the case system and remain the most important missing outcome.

---

## The Halden subset

- **More selected than "survivors twice over".** These organisations completed the pilot, held output records, agreed to follow-up (14 of 23, 61%), and continued with the scheme. The 9 that did not respond may include failures. "Likely optimistic" is more accurate than "upper bound", since record-based measures can err in either direction.
- **The baseline may be wrong.** 40.3 hours is exactly the baseline Varga & Holm reported for all 27 time-tracking organisations. The 17-organisation subset had 40.4. Are these 11 organisations being compared with their own baseline? If not, the 11.8% figure needs recomputing.
- **Report all 14 together.** Give the 24-month figure for all 14 organisations, counting the three that reverted, not just the 11 that continued.
- **One reversion does not fit the Summary's framing.** The Summary says all three reverting organisations had "client-facing or coverage obligations". The marketing agency cited client deadlines. Marketing is discretionary work in the meta-analysis's coding, so this is a reversion in discretionary work. The Summary's framing makes the coverage pattern look cleaner than it is.
- **A Halden author is on this paper,** but the report does not address the re-analysis's finding that Halden's attrition was misreported. It engages with the re-analysis's conclusion while passing over its factual correction. The joint authorship is the natural place to correct the record.

---

## Smaller points

- **The counter arm.** The 7.3 versus 4.0 minute comparison is now against control offices, which is an improvement. Final month-12 estimates for output, repeat contacts and abandoned calls should also be reported. The costing (12% more staff giving 9% higher cost per contact) implies labour is about 75% of cost per contact; state that assumption.
- **Sick days.** The figure (−27%) still isn't expressed per scheduled day, so the share caused simply by fewer scheduled days is unknown.
- **Uncertainty.** Resignations and appeal-overturn rates are still reported without confidence intervals. The 24-month appeal data at least deal with my earlier concern that appeals had not yet had time to resolve.
- **Inference.** Inference with 7 offices per arm still isn't described. A wild cluster bootstrap or randomisation inference is needed.
- **The meeting-audit observation.** The interpretation is appropriately cautious. The final point is well made: no arm reorganised without cutting hours, so the trial cannot separate "reorganisation causes the gain" from "cutting hours is what forces reorganisation to happen".

---

## Bearing on the earlier documents

| Earlier claim | Status after this report |
|---|---|
| Halden: +23% per hour, applies across sectors | Not supported. About +8–10% on the strictest measures, and coverage-bound work loses output |
| Varga & Holm: gains "entirely an artifact" | Not supported. +8.5% (3.4 to 13.8) under randomisation, record-based output and log-measured hours over two years |
| Varga & Holm: meetings hypothesis is post hoc | Partly answered. Survives a registered test, but within the same offices that generated it |
| Meta-analysis: "no sign of decay" | Not supported. The four long studies were uncontrolled and used scheduled hours. Modest, untested decline here, partly confounded by the control group's changes |

---

## Bottom line

The report moves the evidence forward and its rebuttals are fair. A conclusion the data support would be:

> In public-sector case processing, cutting scheduled hours by 20% left output per log-measured hour about 8–9% higher after two years, with output per employee about 3% lower (not statistically significant). Much of the per-hour gain is associated with cutting recurring meetings, which may be achievable without reducing hours. Durability beyond two years and generality beyond one employer remain open.

Before publication, the authors should:
1. Fix the mixed-measure comparison in the Summary.
2. Analyse the control group's mid-trial change.
3. Replace "confirms" with "supports" and explain how the mediation intervals handle clustering.
4. Define what system-log time measures.
5. Report backlog and deadline data.
